knowledgePoints.name: Four reasons, and only four
knowledgePoints.teach:
Delegation costs a round trip, a fresh context, and a summary in place of detail. It is worth paying for exactly four reasons:

  • Context isolation — verbose exploration stays out of the main window. A research agent can read fifty files without fifty files landing in your conversation.
  • Parallelization — independent subtasks finish in the time of the slowest, not the sum.
  • Specialized instructions — expertise that would be noise in the main prompt.
  • Tool restrictions — a doc reviewer holding only Read and Grep cannot modify anything, structurally.

If none of the four applies, a subagent is overhead with extra steps.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four reasons to delegate to a subagent?
options: Getting a cheaper per-token rate for the subtask
Keeping verbose exploration out of the main context
Making a capability impossible by withholding tools
Running independent subtasks alongside each other
questions.explain: You can set a cheaper model per agent, but price is not why the pattern exists — and a subagent is not billed at a discount for being one.

questions.q: A subagent is given only Read and Grep. What happens when it 'wants' to edit a file?
options: It asks the parent process for permission first
It errors, and the parent sees a permission denial
It falls back to Bash and edits the file anyway
Nothing — the tool is not in its session at all
questions.explain: Withholding a tool is not a denial. The tool simply does not exist in that session: no prompt, no error, no mention.

reviewQuestions.q: Name the reason to delegate that has nothing to do with tokens or speed.
options: Specialized instructions and tool restriction
Cheaper per-token billing for the work
Higher rate limits for the subagent's calls
Automatic retries whenever a tool fails
reviewQuestions.explain: Two of the four reasons are about capability shaping rather than resource use.

knowledgePoints.name: Three sources and the precedence rule
knowledgePoints.teach:
1. Programmatically — the agents option on query(). Recommended for SDK apps: the definition ships with the code.
  2. Filesystem — markdown files in .claude/agents/. Shared with anyone using the CLI in that repo.
  3. Built-in general-purpose — Claude can spawn it with no definition at all.

Programmatic definitions take precedence over filesystem agents with the same name.

That precedence is what makes a shipped product predictable: a developer's local .claude/agents/reviewer.md cannot quietly replace the reviewer your app defines.

questions.q: A repo has .claude/agents/reviewer.md and the app passes agents: { reviewer: {...} }. Which definition runs?
options: The filesystem one, because disk always wins
The programmatic one, which takes precedence
Both of them, merged together field by field
Neither — the name collision raises an error
questions.explain: Programmatic wins. That is what makes a shipped agent immune to whatever is in someone's working copy.

questions.q: Which subagent can Claude spawn with no definition anywhere?
options: general-purpose
research-assistant
None — every subagent needs a definition
reviewer
questions.explain: general-purpose is built in. Explore and Plan are also built in, but they are one-shot and return no agentId.

reviewQuestions.q: Which definition source should a shipped SDK product prefer, and why?
options: Programmatic, so it ships with the code unshadowed
Filesystem, so ops can tune agents without a deploy
Built-in general-purpose, to avoid the maintenance
Whichever definition the CLI happened to use last
reviewQuestions.explain: Reproducibility again — the same reason production apps pass settingSources: [].

knowledgePoints.name: The two required fields
knowledgePoints.teach:
AgentDefinition requires exactly two fields:

  • description — natural language saying when to use this agent. This is what Claude matches against when deciding whether to delegate. Write it specifically, the way you would write a tool description.
  • prompt — the subagent's system prompt.

The failure mode follows directly: an agent that is never selected almost always has a vague description, not a broken prompt. "Reviews things" competes with everything; "Reviews Python diffs for SQL injection and unsafe deserialization, before merge" competes with nothing.

questions.q: Claude never delegates to your security-reviewer agent. Which field do you fix first?
options: description — it is what Claude matches against
prompt — it must not be instructing the agent well
model — the agent is too small ever to be selected
tools — Claude skips agents with restricted tools
questions.explain: Selection happens before the prompt is ever used. If the description does not describe the situation you are in, the agent is invisible.

questions.q: Which two AgentDefinition fields are required?
options: name and prompt only
description and tools
prompt and model name
description and prompt
questions.explain: The name is the key you register it under; description and prompt are the required contents.

knowledgePoints.name: The optional fields worth knowing
knowledgePoints.teach:
FieldNotes
toolsAllowed tool names. Omit → inherits every tool available to subagents.
disallowedToolsRemoves tools; accepts MCP patterns mcp__server, mcp__server__*, mcp__*.
modelopus / sonnet / haiku / inherit / full id. Omitted → main model.
skills, memory, mcpServersPreloaded skills; user/project/local memory; per-agent servers.
initialPromptAuto-submitted first user turn only when the agent runs as the main thread agent; ignored as a subagent.
maxTurns, background, effort, permissionModePer-agent turn cap, forced background execution, effort level, permission mode.

questions.q: You set initialPrompt on an agent that is only ever invoked as a subagent. What happens?
options: It is submitted as the subagent's first user turn
It replaces the agent's prompt field entirely
It raises a validation error at construction
It is ignored — initialPrompt is for main agents
questions.explain: Silently ignored. If you need the subagent to start with specific content, it goes in the Agent tool's prompt string instead.

questions.q: Which value of `model` makes a subagent explicitly track whatever the main session is using?
options: 'inherit'
'auto'
'default'
Omitting the field, the only way
questions.explain: Omitting also uses the main model, but 'inherit' says so on purpose — useful when a template might otherwise be given a fixed model.

options: Documentation for your own team to read
The subagent's system prompt at runtime
The label that gets shown for it in the CLI
The text Claude matches on when delegating
reviewQuestions.explain: It is a selection mechanism, not a comment — the same role a tool description plays for tool choice.

knowledgePoints.name: Two objects, two conventions, one file
knowledgePoints.teach:
In Python, AgentDefinition is a dataclass whose field names stay camelCase — disallowedTools, permissionMode, maxTurns, mcpServers, initialPrompt — because they map directly to the wire format shared with the TypeScript SDK.

Meanwhile ClaudeAgentOptions in the same file uses snake_case: disallowed_tools, permission_mode, max_turns.

AgentDefinition(description=..., prompt=..., maxTurns=5)     # correct
AgentDefinition(description=..., prompt=..., max_turns=5)    # TypeError

ClaudeAgentOptions(max_turns=5)                              # correct
ClaudeAgentOptions(maxTurns=5)                               # wrong

Passing the wrong one raises TypeError at construction, not at run time — which is the merciful version.

questions.q: In Python, which object takes max_turns and which takes maxTurns?
options: Both objects take max_turns, as Python usually does
ClaudeAgentOptions max_turns; AgentDefinition maxTurns
AgentDefinition max_turns; ClaudeAgentOptions maxTurns
Both objects take maxTurns, matching the wire format
questions.explain: AgentDefinition keeps camelCase because it maps straight to the wire format shared with TypeScript.

questions.q: Why does AgentDefinition keep camelCase in Python at all?
options: Its fields map onto the wire format TypeScript uses
An oversight that is being fixed in a later release
Python dataclasses are not able to use snake_case
To match the .claude/agents markdown front matter
questions.explain: It is a serialisation boundary showing through. Knowing why makes it stick better than memorising the list.

options: It works exactly as you would expect it to
It works, but the permission mode is ignored
TypeError at construction — it is permissionMode
It constructs fine and raises later, at query time
reviewQuestions.explain: Construction-time TypeError. ClaudeAgentOptions is the one that wants permission_mode.

knowledgePoints.name: Omitted, listed, empty
knowledgePoints.teach:
Three states, three very different agents:

  • tools omitted → inherits every tool available to subagents. Silence means "give them the whole keyring."
  • tools: ['Read', 'Grep'] → exactly those. Anything else is not in the session at all.
  • tools: [] → no tools. The agent can only think and answer.

Common combinations worth recognising: read-only analysis Read, Grep, Glob; test execution Bash, Read, Grep; code modification Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob; full access → omit the field.

disallowedTools subtracts, and accepts MCP patterns: mcp__server, mcp__server__*, mcp__*.

questions.q: You define a doc-reviewer subagent and omit the tools field entirely. What can it do?
options: Nothing at all, until you list some tools
Only Read, Grep and Glob, the safe defaults
It inherits every tool available to subagents
Only the tools the parent put in allowedTools
questions.explain: Omission is maximal, not minimal. Listing is how you restrict.

questions.q: Which tool set makes it structurally impossible for a subagent to modify the repo?
options: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
Read, Grep, Glob
Omit tools and set permissionMode: 'plan'
Read, Edit, guarded by a PreToolUse hook
questions.explain: Bash re-opens every door. Plan mode and hooks are policy layers that can be misconfigured; a missing tool cannot be.

reviewQuestions.q: tools omitted vs. tools: [] — what is the difference?
options: Omitted inherits everything; [] means no tools
No difference; both of them mean default tools
Omitted means none; [] inherits everything there is
Both of them raise a validation error at once
reviewQuestions.explain: One of the confusable pairs the exam likes: absence and emptiness mean opposite things here.

knowledgePoints.name: Delegation happens through a tool, and it must be approved
knowledgePoints.teach:
Claude does not delegate by magic. It calls a tool, and that tool's name must be auto-approved or the delegation silently fails — it falls through to canUseTool, or is denied outright in dontAsk mode.

So a coordinator whose subagents never run, with no error anywhere, is almost always missing the spawn tool from allowedTools.

The tool's name has changed:

  • Current SDK: the tool is Agent. Put "Agent" in allowedTools.
  • It was renamed from Task in Claude Code v2.1.63. Current releases still emit "Task" in the system:init tools list and in result.permission_denials[].tool_name, so detection code should match both.

questions.q: A coordinator's subagents never run and nothing errors. What is the most likely cause?
options: The subagent definitions are invalid somehow
The spawn tool is missing from allowedTools
maxTurns is set too low for the delegation
The subagents have no tools of their own
questions.explain: Silent is the tell. An unapproved spawn tool does not error — the delegation simply never happens.

questions.q: Your parser looks for delegation in the message stream. Which tool names should it match?
options: Only "Agent", the current name
Only "Task", the older name
"Subagent", used in the stream
Both — the old name still appears
questions.explain: Match both. The rename landed in v2.1.63 but the old name persists in several places in the stream.

knowledgePoints.name: The exam answers Task; your code writes Agent
knowledgePoints.teach:
The CCA-F Exam Guide (v1.0, July 2026) predates the rename and names the Task tool.

Glossary term t4 asks what a coordinator's allowedTools must include and keys the answer to "Task".

  • On the exam: answer "Task."
  • In real code: write "Agent", and match both when parsing.

This is the single largest course-versus-exam divergence in Section 8. Hold both answers, and keep straight which context you are in.

questions.q: On the CCA-F exam, what must a coordinator's allowedTools include so it can spawn subagents?
options: "Task"
"Agent"
"Subagent"
"Delegate"
questions.explain: Exam answer: Task. The exam guide v1.0 predates the v2.1.63 rename, and glossary t4 keys to it.

questions.q: You are writing production code today against a current SDK. Which name goes in allowedTools?
options: "Agent", the current tool name
"Task", to match the exam guide
Both of them, listed in an array
Neither — the spawn tool is always approved
questions.explain: "Agent" is the current tool. Listing "Task" as well is harmless but only "Agent" is doing the work; matching both matters when parsing, not when allowing.

reviewQuestions.q: Give both answers to "what is the subagent spawn tool called?" and say which context each belongs to.
options: Agent on the exam, Task in production code
Task on the exam, Agent in production code
Task in both the exam and the current SDK
Agent in both the exam and the current SDK
reviewQuestions.explain: Exam guide v1.0 says Task; the shipping SDK renamed it to Agent in v2.1.63.

knowledgePoints.name: The inheritance table
knowledgePoints.teach:
A subagent's context window starts fresh. It does not inherit the parent's conversation.

It receivesIt does not receive
Its own AgentDefinition.promptThe parent's conversation history or tool results
The Agent tool's prompt stringThe parent's system prompt
Project CLAUDE.md — only if loaded via settingSourcesPreloaded skill content, unless listed in skills
Tool definitions (inherited, or the tools subset)

questions.q: Which of these does a subagent inherit from its parent?
options: The parent's conversation history so far
The parent's own system prompt
The definitions of the tools
The parent's earlier tool results
questions.explain: Tools cross; conversation does not. That asymmetry is the whole design.

questions.q: Under what condition does a subagent see the project CLAUDE.md?
options: Always, in every subagent run
Only if the parent read it into context
Only if settingSources loaded it
Never — CLAUDE.md is main-thread only
questions.explain: The same settingSources rule that governs the main thread governs the subagent.

knowledgePoints.name: The one channel in
knowledgePoints.teach:
The only content that crosses from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string.

Everything the subagent needs — a file path, an error message, a prior finding, a decision already made — must be written into that prompt explicitly. Nothing else carries.

This is exam glossary t6, near verbatim: "How does a subagent receive context from prior research findings?" → the findings must be explicitly included in its prompt.

Practical consequence: a coordinator's job is largely writing good prompts for its workers. A delegation prompt that says "continue the analysis" is a delegation to an agent that has no idea what the analysis was.

questions.q: How does a subagent receive context from prior research findings?
options: It reads the parent's transcript automatically
The findings go explicitly into its prompt
Through shared memory between the two agents
Via the parent's system prompt, which it inherits
questions.explain: Exam glossary t6. The Agent tool's prompt string is the only channel in.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates with the prompt "continue the analysis and report back." What goes wrong?
options: Nothing — the subagent resumes from the context
The subagent errors out on the empty prompt
The subagent has no idea what analysis is meant
It inherits the analysis but none of the tools
questions.explain: It will do something — that is the danger. It will just do it without any of the context the coordinator assumed it had.

reviewQuestions.q: Name the only content that crosses from parent to subagent.
options: The parent's last five messages
The Agent tool's prompt string
The parent's own system prompt
Any file the parent has read
reviewQuestions.explain: One string. Everything else must be written into it.

knowledgePoints.name: Only the final message comes back
knowledgePoints.teach:
Coming back the other way, the parent receives the subagent's final message as the Agent tool result. Intermediate tool calls and their results stay inside the subagent.

That is the entire point. A research-assistant can read fifty files without fifty files landing in the main context — the parent gets the conclusion, not the reading.

One wrinkle: the parent may summarize that final message in its own response. If you need it verbatim — a report, a diff, a list of findings — instruct the main query to preserve it.

questions.q: A research subagent reads 50 files and reports back. What lands in the parent's context?
options: All 50 of the file contents that it read
The subagent's full transcript of the run
Nothing, until the parent asks for it
The subagent's final message, nothing else
questions.explain: Final message only. This is exactly why delegation is the primary context lever.

questions.q: Your coordinator keeps paraphrasing a subagent's carefully formatted report. What is the fix?
options: Set the subagent's model to a bigger one
Tell the main query to preserve it verbatim
Increase maxTurns on the subagent itself
Return the report as a tool_result block
questions.explain: The parent is free to summarise unless told otherwise. Say otherwise.

reviewQuestions.q: What does the parent receive as the Agent tool result?
options: The subagent's full transcript
A structured summary from the SDK
The subagent's final message
A session id to fetch results with
reviewQuestions.explain: Final message. Everything else stayed inside.

knowledgePoints.name: Background by default, three layers deep
knowledgePoints.teach:
Behaviours that changed in v2.1.198:

  • Subagents run in the background by default. An Agent tool call that omits run_in_background launches a background subagent; Claude sets run_in_background: false when it needs the result before continuing. background: true on the definition forces background regardless.
  • A subagent inherits the main session's extended thinking configuration.

Nesting: subagents can spawn subagents three layers deep by default. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH changes it, and 1 turns nesting off.

questions.q: How deep can subagents nest by default, and what changes it?
options: One layer; nesting cannot be turned on
Unlimited; capped only by the maxTurns value
Two layers; set by AgentDefinition.maxTurns
Three; CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH
questions.explain: Three by default. Setting the variable to 1 is how you flatten the topology.

questions.q: Claude needs a subagent's answer before it can continue. What does it do?
options: Sets run_in_background: false on the call
Sets background: true on the definition
Polls the subagent's session id for it
Nothing — subagents always block anyway
questions.explain: Background is the default; blocking is the explicit choice Claude makes when the result is needed inline.

reviewQuestions.q: Since v2.1.198, do subagents block the parent by default?
options: Yes, they always block the parent
No — background unless told to block
Only when they are nested inside another
Only when they have tools of their own
reviewQuestions.explain: Background by default; blocking on demand.

knowledgePoints.name: Detecting delegation in the stream
knowledgePoints.teach:
To show "delegating to research-assistant…" in your own UI:

  • Look for tool_use blocks named "Agent" — or "Task", which still appears in current releases.
  • Messages produced inside a subagent carry parent_tool_use_id. That is how you attribute a message to the right agent.
  • Python reads blocks via message.content; TypeScript via message.message.content — the SDK message wraps the API message.

questions.q: Which field tells you a message came from inside a subagent rather than the main thread?
options: parent_tool_use_id
parent_session_id
is_subagent: true
spawned_by_agent
questions.explain: parent_tool_use_id points back at the Agent tool call that spawned it.

questions.q: In TypeScript, how do you reach the content blocks of an SDK message?
options: message.content
message.data.content
message.message.content
message.content.blocks
questions.explain: The SDK message wraps the API message in TypeScript. Python flattens it to message.content.

knowledgePoints.name: Resuming a subagent
knowledgePoints.teach:
The Agent tool result contains a text block with agentId: <id>. To go back to that same subagent later:

  1. Capture the session_id and the agentId.
  2. Re-query with resume: sessionId, naming the agent in the prompt.

Built-in Explore and Plan agents are one-shot and return no agentId — there is nothing to resume.

Beyond a few agents per turn, the Workflow tool (TS SDK v0.3.149+) moves orchestration into a script that runs outside the conversation context.

questions.q: What two identifiers do you need to resume a specific subagent?
options: The session_id and the agentId
parent_tool_use_id and tool_use_id
The agentId on its own is enough
session_id and the agent's name
questions.explain: Session to get back to the conversation, agentId to name which agent inside it.

questions.q: Why can you not resume an Explore agent?
options: It runs in a completely separate process
Its session is never persisted to disk
It is one-shot and returns no agentId
It has no tools, so there is no state
questions.explain: Explore and Plan are both one-shot built-ins. No agentId, nothing to resume.

options: The system:init message at startup
The AgentDefinition that you wrote
A text block in the Agent tool result
The parent_tool_use_id on the message
reviewQuestions.explain: It comes back with the result, which is why you have to capture it at the time.

knowledgePoints.name: The topology isolation forces
knowledgePoints.teach:
Hub-and-spoke: a coordinator owns all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and routing. Subagents do not talk to each other.

This is not a style preference — it is what context isolation leaves you with. There is no channel between siblings, because the only channel that exists is a parent writing a prompt string for a child.

So when subagent B needs something subagent A discovered, the sequence is always: A returns its final message → the coordinator reads it → the coordinator writes it into B's prompt. (Exam glossary t3.)

questions.q: Three subagents each need a fact the first one discovered. How does it reach them?
options: The first subagent broadcasts it to its siblings
Shared session memory makes it available to all
The coordinator writes it into each later prompt
Each subagent re-derives the fact independently
questions.explain: Hub-and-spoke, forced by isolation. Every fact that moves between workers moves through the coordinator.

questions.q: Why can't you build a mesh of subagents that message each other directly?
options: The SDK rate-limits agent-to-agent calls hard
There is no sibling channel; only the prompt
Mesh topologies need the separate Workflow tool
Only three agents may ever be running at once
questions.explain: The absence of a channel is the architecture. Everything else follows from it.

reviewQuestions.q: Name the coordination pattern in which subagents never communicate directly.
options: Prompt chaining
Evaluator-optimizer
Dynamic decomposition
Hub-and-spoke
reviewQuestions.explain: Glossary t3. The coordinator owns routing, error handling, and every message between workers.

knowledgePoints.name: Fixed sequence vs. discovered subtasks
knowledgePoints.teach:
• Prompt chaining (glossary t12) — fixed sequential decomposition. The steps are known up front: analyse each file, then run a separate cross-file integration pass. Use it when you can write the plan before the run starts.
  • Dynamic / adaptive decomposition (t13) — subtasks generated from what each step discovers. Use it for open-ended investigation: "add tests to a legacy codebase," where you cannot know what needs testing until you have looked.

The discriminating question is simply: could you have written the list of subtasks before starting? If yes, chain. If no, decompose dynamically.

questions.q: "Add tests to this legacy codebase." Fixed chain or dynamic decomposition?
options: Fixed chain — testing is always the same steps
Fixed chain, since the number of files is known
Neither; this is really just a single-agent task
Dynamic — the subtasks depend on what you find
questions.explain: You cannot list what needs testing before you have looked at the code. That is the definition of the dynamic case.

questions.q: "Summarise each of these 12 reports, then write one combined brief." Which shape?
options: Dynamic decomposition, discovered as you go
Prompt chaining — the steps are known up front
Hub-and-spoke, a third option beyond the two
Neither; use a single query for all twelve
questions.explain: Per-item work then an integration pass, all writable in advance. Textbook prompt chaining.

reviewQuestions.q: What single question separates prompt chaining from dynamic decomposition?
options: How many subagents end up being involved
Whether the subtask list could be written first
Whether the agents get to run in parallel
Whether there is a coordinator involved at all
reviewQuestions.explain: Known up front → chain. Discovered as you go → dynamic.

knowledgePoints.name: When every worker succeeds and the answer is still wrong
knowledgePoints.teach:
The coordinator is usually the defect.

The exam's multi-agent research scenario: three subagents each succeed, and the final report covers only one sub-topic. The tempting reads are "a subagent failed silently" or "the aggregation step dropped content." Both are wrong.

The root cause is the coordinator's task decomposition being too narrow — it never asked for the other sub-topics, so nothing was there to aggregate.

The general rule: when every worker succeeds and the aggregate is wrong, look up, not down. Success at each node is evidence that the nodes are fine and the partition is not.

questions.q: Three subagents each return a good report, and the combined answer covers only one sub-topic. Where is the bug?
options: One of the subagents must have failed silently
The aggregation step truncated the results
Context isolation dropped the other findings
The coordinator's decomposition was too narrow
questions.explain: Every worker succeeded — so the workers are not the problem. What was never asked for cannot come back.

questions.q: Which observation most strongly points at decomposition rather than worker failure?
options: One of the subagents timed out part-way through
The coordinator ran out of turns to work with
Every subagent succeeded and the whole is thin
A tool came back with isError set to true on it
questions.explain: Universal success plus an incomplete whole is the signature of a bad partition.

reviewQuestions.q: State the diagnostic rule for multi-agent failure.
options: Always suspect the slowest of the subagents
Retry the whole run with a lot more turns
Blame context isolation before anything else
Workers all fine, aggregate wrong → look up
reviewQuestions.explain: Look up. The coordinator owns the partition, and a bad partition survives perfect workers.
